shipped.outcome_quote: In two studies, we replicate earlier findings showing an effect of task context on children's performance on the AtN

blind_target.authors: Chan, J. Y. C., & Mazzocco, M. M.
blind_target.title: Competing features influence children’s attention to number.
blind_target.evidence_quote: First, we aimed to replicate our original findings (Chan & Mazzocco, 2017) with a different sample of preschoolers and adults, using the AtN task.
blind_target.outcome_quote: The results for number-based matches partially held when the total match score was used as the dependent variable (Figure 2b). Consistent with the best match score analyses, the significant main effect of Salience held, F(1, 89) = 10.16, p = .002, !! " = .102, with adults selecting number-based matches more frequently when alternative choices were of low salience (M = 4.16, SD = 3.00) compared to high salience (M = 3.38, SD = 3.29). The significant main effect of Order also held, F(1, 89) = 5.08, p = .027, !! " = .054, with adults making number- based matches more frequently when low salience trials came first (M = 4.49, SD = 3.17) compared to when high salience trials came first (M = 3.14, SD = 3.04). " = .004.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Both studies confirm the main salience finding, but authors explicitly contrast current results with the original: the adult total-match Salience × Order interaction did not recur, and other order-effect comparisons differ. Statements confirming main effects are individual comparisons rather than an overall verdict overriding these explicit contrasts.

shipped.title_o: Evidence for lifespan extension and delayed age–related biomarkers in insulin receptor substrate 1 null mice
shipped.authors_o: Selman; Lingard; Choudhury; Batterham; Claret; Clements; Ramadani; Okkenhaug; Schuster; Blanc; Piper; Al‐Qassab; Speakman; Carmignac; Robinson; Thornton; Gems; Partridge; Withers
shipped.outcome_quote: we show that, consistent with our previous finding, global deletion of Irs1 significantly extends lifespan in female mice. In addition, an augmented and completed study demonstrates lifespan extension in male Irs1 null mice.

blind_target.authors: Selman C, Lingard S, Choudhury AI, Batterham RL, Claret M, et al.
blind_target.title: Evidence for lifespan extension and delayed age-related biomarkers in insulin receptor substrate 1 null mice.
blind_target.evidence_quote: In the current study we examined lifespan in a second, independent cohort of female WT and Irs1 −/− mice to determine whether our original finding was indeed repeatable.
blind_target.outcome_quote: In conclusion, we replicate and validate our previous finding [12] that global deletion of Irs1 induces a robust lifespan extension in female mice.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Female lifespan extension replicated in an independent cohort. The completed and augmented male cohort instead showed lifespan extension, explicitly contrasted with the original male null result. The concluding confirmation is limited to females, rather than a verdict covering both sexes. Male contrast: We also show that, in contrast to our earlier study [12] , a completed and augmented lifespan study in male mice indicates that median lifespan is extended in male Irs1 −/− mice by ∼16%.

shipped.title_o: Do Neuroscience Journals Accept Replications? A Survey of Literature
shipped.outcome_quote: Of the 131 journals reviewed, only one (0.8%; Journal of Interpretation) explicitly stated that replications were accepted, 108 (82.4%) did not state their position on replications, thirteen (9.9%) implicitly discouraged replications by emphasizing the novelty of manuscripts, none (0%) explicitly stated that replications were rejected, and in nine cases (6.9%), it was not possible to access this information.

blind_target.title: Do Neuroscience Journals Accept Replications? A Survey of Literature
blind_target.evidence_quote:
In a second bibliometric study, a conceptual

replication of Yeung’s (2017) study on the acceptance of replications in neuroscience journals
was conducted by analyzing 131 translation and interpreting journals.
blind_target.outcome_quote:
While the percentage of journals that do not state their
position on this matter or implicitly discourage replications is similar to that in Yeung’s (2017) study

of neuroscience journals, the percentage of journals that explicitly accept replications is larger in

neuroscience (6%) and psychology journals (4%; Martin and Clarke 2017).

shipped.outcome_quote: Results support activation relationship theory by noting a pattern of parenting behaviors used by fathers (and mothers) in which parents are moderately intrusive, challenging, or directive

blind_target.authors: Volling, B. L., Stevenson, M. M., Safyer, P., Gonzalez, R., & Lee, J. Y.
blind_target.title: In search of the father-infant activation relationship: A personcentered approach.
blind_target.evidence_quote: The current study replicated a number of previous studies, including Ryan et al. (2006) who used a diverse sample of low-income couples with a 24-month-old child and the three-bags task, Brady-Smith et al. (2013) who used a sample of low-income mothers with a 12month-old infant and the three-bags task, and Volling et al. (2019) who used a sample of predominantly middle-class couples with a 12-month-old infant and a challenging teaching task.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Interestingly, we found that the proportion of fathers with a supportive parenting profile (55.21%) was greater than that of mothers with a supportive parenting profile (25.91%). This seems inconsistent with previous research, which found that middle-class (Volling et al., 2019) and low-income (Ryan et al., 2006) mothers were more likely than their counterpart fathers to be characterized by supportive parenting.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Activation profile replicated; paper explicitly contrasts the mother/father distribution with this original. The conclusion confirms key profile findings in this regard, rather than giving an overall verdict overriding the contrast.

shipped.title_o: Patient preferences for direct-to-consumer telemedicine services: a nationwide survey
shipped.outcome_quote: Telemedicine ease of use and satisfaction were comparable to in-person visits.

blind_target.authors: Welch BM, Harvey J, O’Connell NS, McElligott JT
blind_target.title: Patient preferences for direct-to-consumer telemedicine services: a nationwide survey
blind_target.evidence_quote: We replicated and extended a previous 2017 survey, developed and reviewed by health care professionals and researchers, to directly compare results [ 14 ].
blind_target.outcome_quote: Such differences between willingness and comfort levels have become easier to see: in the 2017 study, willingness and comfort mirrored one another, while this study saw a distinct separation of the two when looking at the comfort of using telemedicine with a wholly new health care professional—18.6% for both comfort and willingness in 2017, and 33.49% comfort and 33.86% willingness now [ 14 ].
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Authors explicitly report a similar relationship-distance gradient, while contrasting use/awareness and willingness-comfort patterns with 2017. There is no overall verdict that the replication as a whole confirmed the original. The explicit contrast is coded as written even though the numerical willingness/comfort difference is small.
blind_target.additional_support_quote: Welch et al [ 14 ] found that patients became less willing to use telemedicine as they became further detached from their own health care professional in 2017, our study showed a similar trend for both willingness and comfort.

blind_target.outcome_quote:

blind_target.title: Resurgence under delayed reinforcement.
blind_target.evidence_quote: This study aims to (1) replicate Jarmolowicz and Lattal’s (2014) procedure with rats and (2) compare resurgence when delays are introduced without altering reinforcement frequency, isolating the effects of delay from rate changes to clarify conditions for resurgence and refine understanding of how degraded reinforcement contributes to behavioral relapse.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Our results replicated the findings of Jarmolowicz and Lattal (2014) on delayed alternative reinforcement, originally demonstrated with pigeons.

blind_target.title: Forming impressions of personality.
blind_target.evidence_quote:
In the present study, we aimed to both replicate Asch’s 

(1946) finding of a primacy effect in impression formation, and to test the possible role of 

pragmatics in shaping such primacy effects.
blind_target.outcome_quote:
One main finding of this paper is that, while we were unable to detect as strong a primacy effect 

as Asch (1946) originally reported, on balance there is evidence for a primacy effect in 

impression formation.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The authors give an overall on-balance verdict supporting the primacy effect across the paper. This overall assessment takes precedence over individual null studies and the smaller effect.

shipped.authors_o: Deckert; Nöthen; Franke; Delmo; Fritze; Knapp; Maier; Beckmann; Propping
shipped.outcome_quote: Our findings provide evidence for a susceptibility locus for panic disorder, and possibly including agoraphobia, either within the ADORA2A gene or in a nearby region of chromosome 22, and serves as the first successful candidate gene replication study in panic disorder.

blind_target.authors: Deckert J, Nothen MM, Franke P, Delmo C, Fritze J, Knapp M et al
blind_target.title: Systematic mutation screening and association study of the A1 and A2a adenosine receptor genes in panic disorder suggest a contribution of the A2a gene to the development of disease.
blind_target.evidence_quote: Previous work has shown that a silent coding polymorphism (1083C/T, or SNP-4 in this study) in exon 2 in ADORA2A is associated with PD (Deckert et al, 1998). A Japanese group tried to replicate this finding in 87 PD patients, but found no association (Yamada et al, 2001). Given the possible importance of adenosine receptor function in panic, we proposed to study the role of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in or near the ADORA2A gene in a population of patients with PD.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Our findings provide evidence for a susceptibility locus for panic disorder, and possibly including agoraphobia, either within the ADORA2A gene or in a nearby region of chromosome 22, and serves as the first successful candidate gene replication study in panic disorder.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The explicit overall successful replication verdict controls despite absent single-marker association and differences in allele results.
